chapters.title: Responsive Design and Container Queries
chapters.summary: Build layouts that adapt to any screen and any container, with fluid type and responsive images.

lesson.heading: Foundations: mobile-first and intrinsic layout
lesson.body:
Responsive design starts with the viewport meta tag, flexible units and layouts that adapt on their own (flex wrapping, grid auto-fit, `max-width: 100%` on media). Media queries then handle the cases intrinsic layout cannot.

**Mobile-first** means the base styles target small screens and `min-width` queries add complexity as space grows. Benefits: simpler base CSS, small devices download and parse the least override logic, and it forces content prioritisation. Desktop-first uses `max-width` queries and tends to produce more overrides.

Choose breakpoints where **the content breaks**, not at specific device widths. Use `em` or `rem` in media queries so they respect user font-size changes.

lesson.heading: Media queries in 2026
lesson.body:
Modern media queries support **range syntax**, which is clearer than `min-/max-` prefixes and avoids off-by-one gaps: `@media (40em <= width < 64em)`.

Useful media features beyond width:
- `prefers-color-scheme: dark` for system dark mode.
- `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` to tone down animation for users with vestibular disorders.
- `prefers-contrast: more` and `forced-colors: active` (Windows high contrast).
- `hover: hover` and `pointer: fine | coarse` to detect input capability rather than guessing from screen size: touch devices need bigger targets and no hover-only menus.
- `orientation`, `resolution`, `display-mode: standalone` (installed PWAs).

lesson.heading: Fluid sizing with clamp(), min() and max()
lesson.body:
`clamp(MIN, PREFERRED, MAX)` returns the preferred value but never below MIN or above MAX. It replaces stacks of breakpoints for type and spacing.

`font-size: clamp(1.25rem, 1rem + 1.5vw, 2rem)`: at a 1000px viewport the middle value is 16 + 15 = 31px, between 20px and 32px. Mixing `rem` into the preferred value matters: pure `vw` font sizes do not grow when users zoom or increase their default font size, which fails WCAG resize-text requirements.

- `min(100%, 60rem)` picks the smaller value: a container that is full-width on mobile and capped on desktop.
- `max(1rem, 3vw)` picks the larger: spacing that never gets too small.

lesson.heading: Container queries
lesson.body:
Media queries respond to the **viewport**. Components, however, live in containers of different widths: the same card might sit in a narrow sidebar or a wide main column. **Container queries** let a component respond to its container's size. Size container queries are supported in all major browsers since 2023.

- Mark an ancestor as a container: `container-type: inline-size` (queries width) or `size` (width and height; requires explicit height). Optionally name it with `container-name` or the `container` shorthand.
- Query it: `@container card (width > 30rem) { ... }`. Without a name, the nearest ancestor container is used.
- An element cannot query itself; styles inside the query apply to descendants. Containment is what prevents infinite layout loops (the container's size cannot depend on its contents in the queried axis).
- Container query units: `cqi` (1% of container inline size), `cqb`, `cqw`, `cqh`, `cqmin`, `cqmax`.
- **Style queries** (`@container style(--variant: compact)`) query custom property values; supported in Chromium and Safari, not yet in every browser.

lesson.heading: Responsive images
lesson.body: - **Resolution switching**: `srcset` with width descriptors (`640w`) plus `sizes` tells the browser the candidate files and how wide the image will display, so it can choose before layout happens. Without `sizes` the browser assumes `100vw` and may download an image far bigger than needed. - **Art direction**: `` with `` swaps a different crop at different widths. - **Format switching**: ``, then WebP, with the `` as fallback. - Keep `width`/`height` for aspect ratio, `loading="lazy"` for off-screen images, and `fetchpriority="high"` on the LCP image. - In CSS, `object-fit: cover` crops an image to fill its box without distortion; `image-set()` is the CSS equivalent of srcset for backgrounds.

lesson.heading: Practical gotchas
lesson.body:
- `100vw` includes the vertical scrollbar on desktop, so `width: 100vw` often causes horizontal scrolling. Prefer `100%`.
- Never disable zoom with `maximum-scale=1` or `user-scalable=no`; it is an accessibility failure.
- Touch targets should be at least 24x24 CSS px (WCAG 2.2 AA) and ideally around 44x44.
- Use logical properties (`margin-inline`, `padding-block`) so layouts work for right-to-left languages.
- Test on real devices and DevTools device mode, including landscape, zoom at 200% and 400%, and a large default font size.

keyPoints: Mobile-first uses min-width queries layered on simple base styles; pick breakpoints where content breaks.
Range syntax like (40em <= width < 64em) is clearer than min-/max- prefixes.
Query capabilities (hover, pointer, prefers-reduced-motion, prefers-color-scheme), not device names.
clamp() gives fluid type and spacing; include rem in the preferred value so zoom still works.
Container queries need an ancestor with container-type; elements style descendants, never themselves.
srcset + sizes is for resolution switching; <picture> is for art direction and formats.
100vw includes the scrollbar; never disable user zoom.

questions.prompt: Which approach is mobile-first?
options: Base styles for desktop, then @media (max-width: ...) overrides
Base styles for small screens, then @media (min-width: ...) enhancements
questions.explanation: Mobile-first writes the simplest layout as the default and adds features as space grows with min-width (or width >=) queries.

questions.prompt: Why does @container (width > 400px) have no effect on .card's children here?
options: Container queries are not supported in browsers
No ancestor of the children has container-type set
questions.explanation: Container queries look for the nearest ancestor with container-type (or container). Without one, the query matches nothing. Add container-type: inline-size to a wrapper or to .card itself (then its children can respond).

questions.prompt: What is the computed font-size at a 1000px wide viewport (root font-size 16px)?
questions.explanation: The preferred value 4vw is 40px, which is above the maximum 2rem (32px), so clamp returns 32px.

questions.prompt: What does the sizes attribute tell the browser?
options: Which file sizes in KB are available
How wide the image will be displayed in different conditions, so it can pick a srcset candidate before layout
The intrinsic dimensions of the image
questions.explanation: Image selection happens before CSS layout is known. sizes describes the expected display width so the browser can combine it with device pixel ratio and choose a candidate. Without it, the browser assumes 100vw.

questions.prompt: You need a tightly cropped portrait image on phones and a wide landscape crop on desktop. What should you use?
questions.explanation: Different crops are art direction, which is <picture>'s job. srcset alone only offers the same image at different resolutions and lets the browser choose.

questions.prompt: Why can an element not use a container query to style itself based on its own width?
options: It would create a loop: the style could change the size being queried, so queries only style descendants of the container
Only the body can be a container
questions.explanation: Containment stops the container's size from depending on its contents in the queried axis. Styling the container from its own size could change that size, so the spec only applies query styles to descendants.

questions.prompt: On desktop browsers with classic scrollbars, width: 100vw can cause a horizontal scrollbar.
questions.explanation: vw units include the vertical scrollbar width, so 100vw is wider than the available content area. Use 100% instead.

questions.prompt: Setting font-size: 3vw on body text is accessible because it scales with the screen.
questions.explanation: Pure vw values ignore browser zoom and user font-size preferences in many cases, failing WCAG text resizing. Combine with rem inside clamp().

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are valid media features?
questions.explanation: container-type is a property for declaring query containers, not a media feature. The others are standard media features.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: container-type: ___ makes an element a query container for its width only.
questions.explanation: inline-size applies size containment on the inline axis only, so the height can still depend on content. size contains both axes.

questions.prompt: Media queries vs container queries: when do you use each?
questions.answer:
- Media queries respond to the viewport and user environment: page-level layout (sidebar appears at wide widths), and user preferences like prefers-color-scheme, prefers-reduced-motion and pointer type.
- Container queries respond to the size of an ancestor container. They make components truly reusable: a product card can be stacked in a narrow sidebar and horizontal in the main column on the same screen.
- Typical architecture: media queries for the macro layout, container queries for components inside it.
- Requirements: declare container-type: inline-size on a wrapper, query with @container, use cqi units for fluid internals. Remember size containment means the container cannot size itself from its content in that axis.
- Style queries add a way to switch component variants via custom properties, with browser support still incomplete.

questions.prompt: You inherit a desktop-only site. How would you make it responsive?
questions.answer:
- Add the viewport meta tag and audit for fixed widths, absolute layouts and images without max-width.
- Replace fixed pixel widths with fluid ones (%, fr, minmax, max-width with min()), and switch rigid layouts to flex and grid with auto-fit so many cases adapt with no breakpoints.
- Introduce a small set of content-driven breakpoints in em, ideally refactoring toward mobile-first.
- Make typography and spacing fluid with clamp(), and enlarge touch targets for coarse pointers.
- Fix media: srcset/sizes, aspect-ratio, and responsive tables (horizontal scroll wrapper or stacked cards).
- Rework hover-only navigation into a menu button for touch.
- Test on real devices, rotated screens, 200% zoom and RTL if needed, and track CLS and LCP with real-user data.

questions.prompt: How do you optimise images for responsive pages and Core Web Vitals?
questions.answer:
- Use srcset with width descriptors and accurate sizes so phones do not download desktop images.
- Serve AVIF/WebP through <picture> or an image CDN with content negotiation.
- Always set width/height or aspect-ratio to prevent CLS.
- For the LCP image: do not lazy-load it, add fetchpriority="high", make it discoverable in the HTML (not only as a CSS background or injected by JS), and preload if it is referenced late.
- Lazy-load off-screen images with loading="lazy" and use decoding="async" where helpful.
- Compress appropriately, strip metadata, and cache with long-lived immutable URLs.

chapters.title: Modern CSS: Custom Properties, :has(), Nesting and Animation
chapters.summary: Use the modern CSS toolkit for theming, relational selectors, nesting and smooth, performant motion.

lesson.heading: Custom properties (CSS variables)
lesson.body:
Custom properties are declared with two dashes and read with `var()`:
- They **cascade and inherit** like normal properties, so you can override them per component, per theme or per media query: `.card { --pad: 1rem; }`.
- `var(--x, fallback)` uses the fallback when `--x` is not defined.
- They are resolved at **computed-value time**. If the substituted value is invalid for the property (for example `color: var(--size)` where `--size: 20px`), the declaration does not fall back to an earlier rule; it becomes **invalid at computed-value time** and behaves like `unset` (inherited color, for example).
- They are live: changing one with JavaScript (`el.style.setProperty("--x", "10px")`) updates everything that uses it, unlike Sass variables, which are compiled away.
- They cannot be used in media query conditions or selectors.

`@property` registers a custom property with a type, an initial value and inheritance. A registered `<color>` or `<angle>` property can be **animated and transitioned** (for example animating a gradient), and invalid values fall back to the initial value.

lesson.heading: Relational and forgiving selectors
lesson.body:
`:has()` is the long-awaited "parent selector" and much more: it matches an element if the relative selector inside matches something relative to it. It is supported in all major browsers since late 2023.
- `.card:has(img)`: cards that contain an image.
- `form:has(:user-invalid) button[type=submit]`: style the submit button when any field is invalid.
- `h2:has(+ p)`: headings directly followed by a paragraph.
- `body:has(dialog[open])`: lock scrolling while a modal is open.

`:is()` and `:where()` group selectors and are **forgiving**: one invalid selector in the list does not drop the whole rule. `:is()` takes the highest specificity of its arguments; `:where()` is zero. `:not()` accepts complex selector lists.

Other useful modern pseudo-classes: `:focus-visible`, `:focus-within`, `:user-invalid`, `:popover-open`.

lesson.heading: Native CSS nesting
lesson.body:
CSS supports nesting natively (all major browsers since 2023), similar to Sass:
- `&` refers to the parent selector: `&:hover`, `&.active`, `.theme-dark &`.
- Nested element selectors no longer need `&` in current browsers (the "relaxed" syntax): `.card { h2 { ... } }` works.
- Media and container queries can nest inside a rule.
- Unlike Sass, `&` is not string concatenation: `&__title` (BEM suffixing) does not work.
- Nested rules behave like `:is()` for the parent, so specificity follows `:is()` rules.

Keep nesting shallow (two or three levels) to avoid specificity creep.

lesson.heading: Transitions and keyframe animations
lesson.body:
**Transitions** animate between two states when a property changes (hover, class toggle): `transition: transform 200ms ease-out`. Always list specific properties instead of `all`.

**Animations** use `@keyframes` and run on their own: `animation: name duration timing-function delay iteration-count direction fill-mode`. `animation-fill-mode: forwards` keeps the final keyframe's styles after the animation ends; `backwards` applies the first keyframe during the delay.

Animating to and from `display: none` used to be impossible. Now:
- `@starting-style` defines the styles an element starts from when it first renders or goes from `display: none` to shown, enabling entry transitions.
- `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` lets discrete properties like `display` and `overlay` flip at the right moment, so exit transitions finish before the element disappears.

The **View Transitions API** (`document.startViewTransition()`, and cross-document view transitions via `@view-transition`) animates between whole page states.

lesson.heading: Animation performance and accessibility
lesson.body:
The rendering pipeline is style, layout, paint, composite. The cost of an animation depends on which stages each frame triggers:
- `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `margin` trigger **layout** every frame: expensive and janky on large pages.
- `background-color`, `box-shadow` trigger **paint**.
- `transform` and `opacity` can usually run on the **compositor** thread, skipping layout and paint, and stay smooth even when the main thread is busy.

So move things with `transform: translate()`, not `left`; fade with `opacity`; scale with `transform: scale()`.

- `will-change: transform` hints the browser to promote a layer ahead of time. Use it sparingly and briefly; too many layers waste GPU memory.
- `content-visibility: auto` skips rendering work for off-screen sections (pair with `contain-intrinsic-size` to avoid scrollbar jumps).
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`: reduce or remove large motion, parallax and auto-playing animations.

keyPoints: Custom properties cascade, inherit and update live; var() takes a fallback.
A custom property that is invalid for the target property makes the declaration behave like unset, not fall back to an earlier rule.
@property registers a typed custom property so it can be animated.
:has() selects elements based on descendants or following siblings; :where() has zero specificity.
Native nesting uses & and cannot concatenate strings like Sass's &__suffix.
@starting-style and transition-behavior: allow-discrete enable transitions to and from display: none.
Animate transform and opacity for compositor-friendly motion; avoid animating layout properties.
Always honour prefers-reduced-motion.

questions.prompt: What is the width of .box?
questions.explanation: --gap is never defined, so var() uses its fallback, 10px. The --size variable is irrelevant here.

questions.prompt: What color is the text of p?
questions.explanation: The var() substitution is valid at parse time, so the earlier red rule is already overridden in the cascade. At computed-value time 20px is not a colour, so the declaration becomes invalid and acts like unset; color inherits, giving blue.

questions.prompt: Which selector styles cards that contain an image?
questions.explanation: .card img selects the images, not the cards. :has() matches the card when the relative selector inside finds a match. There is no < combinator or :contains() in CSS.

questions.prompt: Which property is cheapest to animate for moving an element horizontally?
questions.explanation: transform skips layout and paint and can be composited off the main thread. left and margin-left trigger layout on every frame.

questions.prompt: Why register a custom property with @property?
options: To give it a type so the browser can interpolate (animate) it and validate values
To use it in media queries
To make it faster to read in JavaScript
questions.explanation: Unregistered custom properties are untyped token streams that can only flip discretely. A registered type such as <angle> or <color> can be interpolated in transitions and animations.

questions.prompt: Which nested selector does NOT work with native CSS nesting the way it does in Sass?

questions.explanation: var() only works in property values. Media query conditions are evaluated without element context, so variables are not allowed there.

questions.prompt: With :has(), CSS can select a parent element based on its children.
questions.explanation: :has() evaluates a relative selector against the element's descendants (or siblings with + and ~), so form:has(input:invalid) targets the form.

questions.explanation: transform and opacity can be handled by the compositor without layout or paint. width, top and margin-left trigger layout on every frame.

questions.prompt: How do CSS custom properties differ from Sass variables? When would you use each?
questions.answer:
- Sass variables are compiled away at build time; the browser only sees the final values. They cannot react to the DOM, media queries at runtime or JavaScript.
- Custom properties live in the browser: they cascade, inherit, can be overridden per element, theme or media query, and update live when changed with JavaScript.
- That makes custom properties ideal for theming (light/dark, brands), design tokens, component APIs (--btn-bg), and values set from JS like a cursor position.
- Sass variables still fit build-time concerns: breakpoint values in media queries (var() is not allowed there), loops and generated utilities.
- Watch out: invalid substitutions behave like unset rather than falling back to earlier rules, so supply fallbacks or register types with @property.

questions.prompt: Why should you animate transform and opacity instead of top/left or width? Tie it to the rendering pipeline.
questions.answer:
- Each frame the browser may run style, layout, paint and composite. Animating left, top, width or margin changes geometry, so layout (and then paint) reruns every frame on the main thread, and can affect many other elements.
- transform and opacity do not affect layout. When the element is on its own layer, the compositor (often on the GPU, in a separate thread) can apply them directly, so the animation stays at 60/120fps even if JavaScript is busy.
- Techniques: move with translate, resize visually with scale, fade with opacity; use FLIP (First, Last, Invert, Play) or the View Transitions API to animate layout changes using transforms.
- Use will-change only right before animating and remove it after, since each layer costs memory.
- Verify with the DevTools Performance panel and Rendering tab (paint flashing, layer borders).

questions.prompt: How would you implement light and dark themes with modern CSS?
questions.answer:
- Define semantic tokens (--bg, --text, --surface, --border, --accent) as custom properties on :root rather than using raw colours in components.
- Respect the OS setting with color-scheme: light dark plus light-dark() values, or @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) overrides.
- Support a manual toggle by setting a data-theme attribute on <html> that overrides the tokens; persist the choice in localStorage and apply it before first paint (a tiny inline script) to avoid a flash of the wrong theme.
- color-scheme also switches native form controls and scrollbars.
- Check contrast in both themes, adjust images and shadows (shadows read poorly on dark backgrounds), and consider color-mix() or oklch() for generating hover and muted shades from one brand colour.

questions.prompt: What can :has() do that was impossible before, and are there caveats?
questions.answer:
- It allows selecting based on descendants or following siblings: style a card differently when it contains an image, a field group when it contains an invalid input, the page when a dialog is open, or a heading followed by a paragraph.
- It replaces many JavaScript class toggles (for example adding .has-error to a parent) with pure CSS that stays in sync automatically.
- Combined with :checked it enables CSS-only state such as theme switchers.
- Caveats: :has() cannot be nested inside another :has(), pseudo-elements are not allowed inside it, and its specificity is that of its most specific argument. Very broad selectors such as body:has(.x) on huge, frequently changing DOMs can cost style recalculation time, so scope it to components where possible.
